podcast.title: Founding (1962)
podcast.body: A&M Records was formed in 1962 by Herb Alpert (the 'A') and Jerry Moss (the 'M'). "They were formed by Herb Albert, the A, and his partner Jerry Moss, who was the M. This was 1962."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Brief Sex Pistols Contract (1977)
podcast.body: Two months after the Sex Pistols were dropped by EMI, A&M Records decided to take a chance and signed them. However, a party at the label's offices following the signing resulted in significant damage, and complaints from other A&M artists like The Carpenters, along with questions from head office in Los Angeles, led to the band being dropped after just six days, with a £75,000 buyout. "Two months later, an M records decided to take a chance and signed the pistols to another deal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 4

podcast.title: Brief Sex Pistols Signing (1977)
podcast.body: In early 1977, A&M Records signed the Sex Pistols after EMI dropped them, but the deal lasted only five days due to rebellion from other A&M artists who refused to be on the same label as the "Yabos," leading management to drop the band. "After being dropped by EMI records because of their bad behavior, they were picked up by A&M records. And that deal lasted for a total of five days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Valuable Vinyl

podcast.title: Destruction Order for "God Save the Queen" (1977)
podcast.body: Following the termination of their contract with the Sex Pistols in 1977, A&M Records ordered the pressing plant to destroy all 25,000 copies of the "God Save the Queen" 7-inch single that had been pressed on the A&M label. "When that contract was terminated, A&M ordered the pressing plant to destroy any and all copies of the God saved the queen seven inch that had been pressed up on A&M records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Valuable Vinyl

podcast.title: Sex Pistols "God Save the Queen" Release and Destruction (1977)
podcast.body: A&M Records signed the Sex Pistols for a mere five days in 1977, during which time approximately 25,000 copies of their "God Save the Queen" 7-inch single were pressed. Following the band's dismissal due to other artists' objections, these singles were ordered destroyed, though several dozen were "liberated" and became highly valuable collectibles. "But in that five days, A&M had pressed up something like 25,000 copies of God Save the Queen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Book of World Records Version 1.0 - Part 2

podcast.title: Sex Pistols Contract and Termination (March 1977)
podcast.body: A&M Records signed the Sex Pistols to a 150,000-pound deal on March 10, 1977, in front of Buckingham Palace in London, only to drop them six days later. The termination was prompted by the band's extensive trashing of the A&M offices after the signing and negative feedback from other artists on the label, such as Captain & Tennille. Despite the termination, the Sex Pistols still walked away with 75,000 pounds. "Six days later, ANM announced that they were dropping the band in part due to the flak they were getting from other acts on the label, acts like the captain and tenel."

podcast.title: Sex Pistols Signing Incident – March 10, 1977
podcast.body: The Sex Pistols signed their record deal with A&M Records outside Buckingham Palace on March 10, 1977. This event was a significant moment in the band's history before their notoriously brief and tumultuous career. "Sid really got into being a sex pistol. He was there when the pistol signed their record deal with A&M records outside of Buckingham Palace in March 10th, 1977."

podcast.title: Connection to "Never Say Never Again" Theme (1983)
podcast.body: A&M Records is mentioned in the context of Lani Hall, the singer of the "Never Say Never Again" theme, being married to Herb Alpert, who was associated with the label. This highlights a link between a major music label and a specific, albeit less remembered, Bond theme. "She was married to her Belpert, the A and A and M records."

podcast.title: Insistence on Publishing Credit for Sting (1985)
podcast.body: When A&M Records learned that Sting had not only guest vocalized on Dire Straits' "Money for Nothing" but that the song also interpolated the melody of a Police hit ("Don't Stand So Close To Me"), they insisted that Sting be added to the song's publishing credits. "However, when And M records got word not only that Sting was a guest on Money for Nothing, but that the Dire Straits song interpolated the melody of a police hit. They insisted that Sting be added to the song's publishing credits."

podcast.title: Acquisition by Polygram (1989)
podcast.body: A&M Records was bought by Polygram in 1989, marking the end of its independent status. "By the time they were bought by Polygram in 1989, they were the biggest indie label in the world."

podcast.title: Largest Indie Label (Pre-1989)
podcast.body: By the time it was acquired by Polygram in 1989, A&M Records had grown to become the biggest independent record label in the world. "By the time they were bought by Polygram in 1989, they were the biggest indie label in the world."

podcast.title: Catalyst for OMD's US Success (1980s)
podcast.body: OMD's move to A&M Records in the United States marked a turning point in their North American career. Unlike their previous label which showed little interest, A&M actively promoted them, leading to increased exposure and success. "We got, um, the biggest change for us actually happened just before that when we changed record labels because the record label we were on in the States couldn't get us arrested and didn't care. We moved to A&M and that's when they started to push us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Challenges for Canadian A&M in US Market
podcast.body: Having the same label name, such as A&M Records, across both Canada and the United States did not provide a Canadian act with an inherent advantage in the American market. In some cases, it was even a "detriment" as the US counterpart might "take it for granted" that the Canadian branch was "part of the family," potentially reducing the urgency or effort to promote their artists. "The fact that your name is A&M Records and their name is A&M Records is not an edge in any way. In fact in some cases it's probably a detriment because they take it for granted, you're part of the family."

podcast.title: Destruction of "God Save the Queen" Single
podcast.body: Following the Sex Pistols' short-lived and controversial contract, A&M Records ordered the destruction of all copies of the band's first single for the label, "God Save the Queen." This decision was part of the label's efforts to sever ties and mitigate the fallout from their brief and tumultuous association with the punk band, making the few surviving copies highly valuable to collectors. "Meanwhile, all copies of the first ANM single, God Save the Queen, were ordered to destroy it."

podcast.title: Embrace of Experimental Artists
podcast.body: During the late 1960s and early 1970s, A&M Records, headquartered in Los Angeles, was notable for its progressive stance, openly embracing "hippie ideals" and readily signing artists deemed weird or experimental, such as Captain Beefheart. "It was headquartered in Los Angeles and had no trouble with the hippie ideals of the day. You're weird, you're experimental, great, what you got, maybe we'll get you a deal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Kings of Quirk

podcast.title: Embrace of Hippie Ideals and Experimentation (Late 60s/Early 70s)
podcast.body: Headquartered in Los Angeles, A&M Records was known for its openness to the prevailing hippie ideals of the late 1960s and early 1970s. The label showed a willingness to sign and indulge experimental and unconventional artists, exemplified by their long-term support for Captain Beefheart despite his eccentricities. "It was headquartered in Los Angeles and had no trouble with the hippie ideals of the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Kings of Quirk

podcast.title: Mainstream & Alt Rock Roster
podcast.body: While known for mainstream and "middle of the road" acts like The Carpenters, A&M Records also contributed to the world of Alt Rock by signing artists such as OMD, Human League, and The Police. They notably dropped the Sex Pistols after only five days. "Most of their acts were pretty mainstream and pretty middle of the road. This was a label of the Carpenters after all. And the company that dropped the Sex Bistles after just five days."

podcast.title: Package to Donna Halper
podcast.body: A&M Records' Canadian arm played a role in Rush's breakthrough by having promoter Bob Roper send a package containing Rush's record to DJ Donna Halper at WMMS Cleveland. The package noted that no label, including A&M Canada, was interested in signing the band. "She got a package from a friend named Bob Roper, who was a promoter with Canada's arm of A&M records."

podcast.title: Police Signing and Releases
podcast.body: Miles Copeland secured The Police a signing with American label A&M Records based on the strength of "Roxanne." A&M later released "Can't Stand Losing You" in England when "Roxanne" was banned, and eventually re-released "Roxanne" in the UK following its US breakthrough. "On the strength of Roxanne alone, Miles got the band signed to American label A&M Records."

podcast.title: Post-Hit Pressure
podcast.body: Following the success of Ozark Mountain Daredevils' "Jackie Blue," A&M Records pressured the band to replicate the hit with similar "Jackie Red," "Jackie Green," and "Jackie Brown" songs. The label also pushed for the band to move to Los Angeles for greater TV exposure, requests the band ultimately refused to protect their artistic integrity and family-centric lifestyle in Missouri. "A and M that's our label said to us Jackie Blue was great now give us Jackie red."

podcast.title: Promoting "Don't You Want Me" in the US
podcast.body: The Human League's US label, A&M Records, "pushed the single hard at radio" after record executives noticed spikes in sales in US towns with MTV. This effort helped "Don't You Want Me" finally enter the Hot 100 in March 1982 and reach number one. "The human leagues US label, A&M Records, pushed the single hard at radio, and it finally entered the hot 100 in March of 1982."

podcast.title: Publicity Stunt Success
podcast.body: A&M's marketing department inadvertently benefited from a publicity stunt for The Flying Burrito Brothers' "Gilded Palace of Sin" album release, where packages of hay were sent out and tested by the USPS for marijuana. The resulting media buzz and seizure created an image of "psychedelic cow punks" that was "better than anything the A&M marketing department could have dreamed up." "The media buzz, the seizure created was better than anything the A&M marketing department could have dreamed up."

podcast.body: At the time of the "Underdogs" album's release, the head A&R executive at A&M (or Universal), Paul A. Graham, made an office bet that the album would not sell more than 30,000 records.
